A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers
I drift off into a world of my own
make sure never to be alone with another person

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
I feel like an object, not like a person
You can never know who will harm you

Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items
issues.explanation: The profile contains several items implying an active sense of present threat or exposure (e.g., 'World is Dangerous', 'Exposed to Others', concealment to avoid being noticed), yet the Threat component is entirely absent. For this trauma type, such items would usually cohere with at least some explicit threat content; the omission makes the cross-node picture clinically uneven.

'World is Dangerous' expresses a broad ongoing threat belief, but the formulation specifies no active links into or out of Threat and no Threat items are endorsed. This makes the appraisal sit awkwardly in the formulation because it functions more like a threat belief than an isolated negative self-appraisal.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
issues.explanation: 'Concealing Clothing ... to avoid being noticed' implies active management of current interpersonal threat/visibility. With Threat completely unrepresented and no Trigger→Threat or Maladaptive Strategies→Threat linkage in the formulation, this strategy lacks a clear matching symptom target in the rest of the profile.

Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: The Threat node is not clinically coherent here. 'Flashbacks' and 'Physical Reactivity' are re-experiencing/arousal responses rather than threat appraisals, while the only genuine threat appraisal selected is 'Threat from Strangers.' That mixes different constructs within one node.

vignette:
Ethan is a 25-year-old single man who works as a housekeeper in a midrange hotel, where much of his day is spent moving alone through dim hallways, stripping beds, sorting towels, and entering rooms that are temporarily empty of other people. He came to treatment after months of telling himself he could manage if he just stayed careful enough, only to find that his life had narrowed around that effort. The experiences he circles back to began in childhood, when he was physically abused by a caregiver in the home at night. He remembers waking in the dark before he fully understood where he was, hearing movement in the room, and then the abrupt certainty that something bad was about to happen. What stands out to him is not a single detail but a sequence that returns like a film: the darkness, the sound of crying elsewhere in the house, and the feel of a particular rough household fabric against his skin while he was being handled. Even now, when he tries to say more, he becomes flooded so quickly that he has to stop talking, pressing his palms into his knees and staring at the floor until the feeling passes.

As he grew older, Ethan found that the memories did not stay in the past. If he wakes in the night and the room is still dark, there are moments when he feels as if he is back there again, not merely remembering but reliving it across his senses all at once. He has described the shift as instantaneous: his chest tightens, his body goes cold and then hot, and for a few seconds he is no longer certain he is in his own apartment. The same thing can happen when he hears children crying nearby. Passing a family in a grocery store or hearing a child crying through the hotel corridor can jolt him into a state of intense alarm, his whole body reacting before he has time to think. Certain textures are just as potent. Handling a rough towel or blanket at work can stop him in place because the sensation seems to pull the old scene forward in full detail. On those occasions he becomes so watchful that he scans the hallway, checks who is nearby, and struggles to continue with what he was doing.

He has come to believe that danger is never far away and that there is no reliable way to know who might turn harmful. He watches people closely, especially in enclosed or private spaces, and he is most uneasy when he might be alone with one other person. At work he lingers near the carts or times his rounds to stay within sight of coworkers, even if it makes him slower. If a supervisor asks him to clean an isolated section late in the day, he sometimes finds a reason to trade assignments or leaves tasks unfinished. Over time, this has affected how dependable he seems on the job. He knows he is dropping responsibilities, and he hates that about himself, but to him it feels reckless not to organize his day around staying safe.

Outside work, he has shaped his life in similar ways. He avoids being alone with others whenever he can, preferring public places or group settings, and if an interaction begins to feel too close or exposed, he mentally disappears into elaborate fantasy. He describes drifting into a world of his own where he does not have to feel his body or the room around him. This can happen on the bus, during breaks, or in the middle of conversations, and afterward he often realizes he has missed what someone said. He is embarrassed by how far away he goes, but he also experiences it as one of the only ways to get through moments that feel unbearable.

What weighs on him most is not only fear but the sense that something about him is visible. Ethan has come to believe that other people can look at him and somehow tell what happened. When guests or coworkers glance at him for too long, he feels exposed, as though the history is written on him. He speaks about himself at times as if he were an object that things were done to rather than a person who had choices. That feeling becomes especially strong after a flashback, when he is left shaken and ashamed, trying to finish cleaning a bathroom or remake a bed while pretending nothing happened.

He sought help after waking in the dark in his apartment and having such a vivid reliving episode that he knocked over a lamp and spent the rest of the night sitting upright, unable to go back to sleep. The next day at work, a child crying in the hallway and the feel of a towel in his hands brought the scene back again, and he had to leave a room half-finished. He is frightened that his world will keep getting smaller, that he will lose his job if he cannot hold himself together, and that he will never feel safe around other people. At the same time, what he hopes for is simple and urgent: to be able to wake up in the dark and know where he is, to do his work without feeling ambushed by his own senses, and to feel like a person again rather than something exposed and waiting to be harmed.
